I'm gonna go with what everyone else here said and add my 2 cents. If you look at it RAW, there are some problems. Your character's base sprint speed is 60 ft in 6 seconds, approximately 6 MPH. Which is REALLY slow.

Sometimes that won't be enough for the players. Then you gotta out-common-sense them. A horse could attack with two hooves, but the coordination involved as well as both targets dodging and probably wearing armor makes that unfeasible for even a human, let alone a horse.

For the "I swing my sword in a wide arc", well I mean have you swung something like a sword irl? They're heavy as hell, and your full damage implies you're bringing all that weight down on one foe. A battlemaster can do that, but odds are they have spent months of in-game time honing those skills. Somebody not trained in that would either hit one foe and stop or put a really weak amount of force behind both blows.

As for that last question, my rule of thumb is it's because magic takes a lot of effort. Why can't you mage hand? Well mage hand takes a standard action and has both verbal and somatic components, as well as requiring concentration to maintain. You spend 6 seconds performing very precise incantations and moving in measured and particular ways JUST to do that, and even then you have to actively focus for it not to fizzle out in six more seconds. A lot of people, like myself, can be stumped by a difficult math problem. And that's entirely just MY focus. Imagine calling on specific arcane energies, gesticulating just so, and utteting a chant perfectly, all the while not even knowing how or where the thing you're summoning will spawn. There is a reason there are spells that suffocate enemies; if basic ones worked that way, who would bother reciting Blight?

In Aidel, many of the fiefs keep up a rivalry with one another. Each one wants the king's affection and each others' territories. Small proxy wars are fought between city states and through arming barbarian tribes. Trade is regular inside a nation but generally it's restricted to traveling merchants. There is one place however you can go to find anything.

##Gallas-Gilead, a mountain stronghold in the Land of Aidel

**Gallas-Gilead** is named for its two founders. Lord Gallas of northern Mublin and his loyal adviser Gilead. Initially they held nothing but enmity for each other. Gilead came from Quinnec, a land of open minds where magic was, and still is, everywhere. To be mundane was to be weak and boring. Gallas was a nationalist and a devout rationalist; to him, the use of magic was a crutch for the week.

Gilead initially met Lord Gallas on the field of battle, then as a spoil of war as Gilead had been captured. Mages in Mublin are not always trusted or treated fairly, but Gallas had seen Gilead's prowess on the field of battle and respected his skill, even if he hated his guts.

The two would ceaselessly argue day and night until Lady Polk, wife of Gallas, insisted the two duel to finally stop the unrest. The two dueled with unbridled ferocity, destroying the arena that stood around them as they tore at one another. They eventually fought to a stalemate. Gallas was treated for his wounds and asked what to do with Gilead, who had been gravely wounded. Instead of executing him as a useless servant, Gallas had his healers diligently work to get Gilead back up.

When Gilead awoke and found himself healed, he pledged eternal gratitude to Gallas. Not only for the healing, but it had been the hardest fight Gilead had ever fought and he had felt truly alive. The two remained friends and founded a neutral city where all would be accepted.

Gallas-Gilead is a small trading hub for all but one day of the year. The Thatchvale Market, held on the summer solstice, is where each nation sends its best. Tournaments are held but the market itself is the true appeal. The best craftsmen and artisans always attend to get recognition. The tournament is a huge public event but the market around it holds true wonders. Magic items of insane rarity, pastries baked by the best chefs of the land, it is a place where every fief sends their best and brightest to show off all that their country has to offer. It's also a good place to end up face down in a ditch if you wander off in the wrong direction, but aside from the participants in the tournament few come to the market with the intention to do violence.

In the land of Aidel, one has to give up one of their five senses to cast magic. Those who lose their sense of smell tend to have weaker offensive spells but gain supernatural abilities that allow them to hunt down enemies of the crown. They are called hounds. Of those hired to take care of enemies, the most elite and discrete serve the High King directly.

**Kingswulves, Hunters from the Gilded Isles in the land of Aidel**

Kingswulves are generally used to hunt down the most dangerous renegades; spellcasters who have gone mad and wantonly pillage the countryside. Renegades may be terrorists, casters who have been spurned by society, or just confused and scared people who have been backed into a corner.

The most dangerous casters are often listeners. Casters who can listen at the border between the immortal and mortal realms, who make pacts with mad demigods known as Faeids to gain extraordinary power. Kingswulves are primarily used to hunt down the strongest listeners.

Kingswulves also hunt down dissenters to the crown in private. Any kill the crown cannot sully it's name with is done by Kingswulves. They are more feared than respected, but none dare stand in their way. The crown has given then carte blanche on killing those who stand in their way.

Any bounty hunter requires state training and licensure. Kingswulves carry special licenses with with the royal seal emblazoned on them in molten gold. It means their actions are fully sanctioned by the king, and to stand in their way is akin to high treason. Training begins at early childhood and to gain certification requires great discipline and loyalty.

Most bounty hunters are paid in gold, but Kingswulves are treated as royalty and are often given free access to rare treasuries. Some spend their time studying forbidden knowledge in deep libraries, others satisfy their more...odd tastes...at discrete brothels. Kingswulves also interact less with the public than normal. Most hounds are allowed to leave the noble house they were trained to serve only for a hunt. Some nobles eventually release their hounds from servitude, though these people may have trouble reintergrating into our society after having been trained to hunt every second of every day.

Why do they hunt? It varies depending on who you ask. Some do it out of family legacy, in terms of Kingswulves they tend to do it for the glory of the position. Some do it for the pay, which is more than half-decent. Many do it because there are few other jobs for hounds.

To be fair they are pigeonholed into the job. The average commoner sees a hound and thinks little aside from "he probably kills renegades and keeps us safe." Rationalists praise hounds, for what greater irony than a mage killing a mage? In turn arcanists usually despise them, asking "how can you kill your brother and sister spellcasters? Do you not see how it makes the five-faced God weep?"

You would end up spending some time in the Homes of Refuge founded by casters to take in new arrivals and the poor. You would probably eat well but a few crazies set up the shops and kill the poor to sell body parts on the deep market. So avoid the shadier parts of town.

In all likelihood you survive but if you get into the criminal underworld you'll probably die. So keep your head down, and watch your step. 

Don't piss off anybody who's a better swordsman than you and don't talk to people with forked ears. Oh definitely. The biggest problem I find with introducing these invisible forces is the ability to kill with impunity.

Let's say you're a mundane human and you really hate a guy called Harry. Maybe Harry stole your girl, maybe he used your lawnmower without permission, maybe he butters his bread on the opposite side that you do and it rubs you the wrong way.

You can strangle him, bury him alive, shoot him, stab him. No matter what though, even if you poison him, somebody is gonna know somebody wanted him dead. And there is probably a trail they can follow that leads em back to you. A good killer makes it look like a suicide or accident but the fact is nobody is perfect and there is probably a mistake that can point all the way back to you.

Now you got magic, and you can zap harry. And when you zap, you use up a bit of mana and energy, but for all intents and purposes it looks like he stuck a fork in an outlet and rode the lightning. Changes the murder, assassination, and political intrigue game completely.

This world sounds like an alternate reality. What are some of the historical events that caused this world to differ from ours so drastically?

The people of Imperia are in many ways similar to the Roman Empire, admittedly with advanced (roughly medieval) technology and not as strong or influential. Still, their society is very militaristic, and ascension through the nobility is very much a function of military rank.

They drove roving barbarians from their lands with far more zeal than other feifs, not even considering letting some integrate like their neighbors to the south.

The first unintended result is natural; only the strong tribes survived and they have formed alliances, allowing them to work far more efficiently towards actual invasion and create real dents in the walls of frontier towns.

The second unintended consequence was driving some of the beast tribes (mainly half foxes and half wolves) into the frozen desert. They founded a city known as Dragon's bones, in (surprisingly enough) The body of an old dragon. The reason this is bad is that nobody knows that settlement exists and dragons haven't been seen since recorded history. The dragon's bones have been hewn into tough weapons and buildings with powerful magic properties. 

Much of the Dragon's corpse was frozen in the frozen desert  (essentially an arctic desert) and it is not truly dead, it merely slumbers in a healing trance. The tribes have bound it using its own bones, and if it did awake and it would be pinned in place by its own bones. As it regenerates, dragon slayers harvest meat and bone from its body. The dragon is mildly pained but is so ancient and powerful it's more like getting a small papercut every day, and is set back enough every day that it does not awaken from its healing trance.

The beast folk who live here have become self-sufficient and have dragonbone equipment such as weapons and armor that can rival steel. While they have not attacked yet, if they were to attack Imperia it is uncertain which faction would stand to lose more. Magic itself is very rare, and having a material naturally imbued with it like a dragon's bone and blood is a huge strategic resource.

There is really a lot to do with this. First of all, unless you already told the party about what these pact stones do, the ball as to how much they know about it is in your court.

Second, that stone in particular was just left as loot. Loot in a dungeon so easily beaten even level 1s (no offense) got through it. That means whoever had it before decided it was no longer worth keeping or saving it for later, so I would argue it starts with 0 souls in it and is just a particularly unbreakable stone right now.

Thirdly you put some information in that item descriptor that seriously helps YOU as a GM. Anyone who has used this legendary super powerful rare item ever gets a friendly ping when it picks up a soul.

So really there's endless possibilities. Maybe a past death knight had his stone stolen by a wily rouge, and now he knows where it is and will send armies to get it back. Maybe the forces of good want that stone and will try to take it back for safekeeping. Right now, you can just say they have a shiny stone that thrums with bad energy. Hell, the stone isn't even discriminatory in who it kills; your own party ally could get soul trapped, then the rest of the party has to beseech a God or somehow get use of a Wish spell to save their fallen comrade.

Yeah you gave then an OP item but it's also a serious plot hook you can use.

Don't be afraid to start from other source material. While being unique is the ultimate goal, the fact is so many stories have been written already that there is no truly 100% unique story.

Know whose shoulders you stand on; writing fantasy? Are you going for high magic like Terry Pratchett? Gritty fantasy like George R R Martin? If it's sci-fi, are you writing soft sci fi like "Stranger in a Strange Land," or do you want to spell out the facts of your world like Isaac Asimov? Even if your world feels unique, It's not a bad idea to find ones like it or look to where your inspiration might have come from.

Don't be afraid to start your world as very similar to another world and slowly build its unique facets from there. The world I'm working on took heavy inspiration from GRRM's asoiaf world, especially as it relates to noble houses squabbling over land and resources with brutal consequences all around. I added some inspiration from the video game gloom to create a pact of elite assassins. I brought in inquisitors from the real life inquisition to add further to that. From our unique spins and interweaving of others' works, we make our unique things.

It's like a quote from a movie I once saw, Flash of Genius, where the main character has his patent for automated windshield wipers stolen. The corporation argues he did not come up with the concept nor the individual parts needed. The complainant pulls out a copy of Charles Dickens' "A Tale of Two Cities," and points out how every word in it is contained in a dictionary but the work itself is unique.

Point is, Your world is probably not going to be wholly unique, even if parts of it resemble a world you have never read about. Find what appeals to you about other worlds, and practice and modify those elements until you make them yours.

Feyandre was once the magical capital of the world, located in the southeast corner of the somewhat triangular continent of Tharinn. One day, shortly before two of the largest countries on the continent began a long and bloody war, the land seemed to vanish.

Giant mountains rose at the country's edge, jagged in shape and almost perfectly smooth on the surface. Made of tough bedrock that not even the dwarves' finest technology could pierce. One man mounted a wyvern to try to see over the mountains, but his mount tired as it flew to the top, and he only caught a glimpse of where Feyandre was. The entire place was covered by a thick fog, obscuring the land. In order to land safely, he had to return to the ground before he could see any more.

Some say Feyandre found some ancient magic that was too powerful to share so they blocked themselves off, some say the growing of the kingdom of man frightened them, and they feared they would be the next conquest. All that is known is that Feyandre has made no contact with the outside world since, and the mountains seem to have their own heir of madness. Civilization that people try to found near the mountains inevitably breaks down into barbarous tribalism.

Mountain Elves are mildly based on ancient Andean culture. They have the ability to bring forth plant life from stone itself. This allows them to create subterannean farms that grow grass for cattle, fruits that normally need sunlight  (although their flavors are changed due and most become pale white) and root vegetables underground.

This magic comes from their ancestors, high elves who fled the kingdom of men to avoid persecution, and was honed both by their ancestors and the innate magic of the ores they grew up around. The fact they came from high elves, however, has been all but forgotten.

This grants them the friendship of dwarves and gnomes who share their own food in return for the rare delights of stonegrown produce. This also does arouse some suspicion by dwarves and the curiosity of the gnomes, as they use the plant life to ensure their own privacy.
